name: Flor de ruina
classification_notes: Built as five sequential glyph states, germen, semilla, flor, ruina and fractura, tracing a flower's life cycle from germination to fracture. Pixel-edged construction and a brutalist rawness deliberately slow the reader down.
summary: A five-stage pixel display face that grows, blooms and fractures like a flower, built to interrupt automatic reading.
description: Flor de Ruina moves through five linked states, from germen to fractura, each glyph set further along a botanical life cycle than the last. Felipe Sanzana built it as a tool for slow reading, deliberately unsettling the automatic pace most typefaces aim for. Pixel-edged forms and a brutalist rawness carry that intent through into the letterforms themselves.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Flor de Ruina as emerging from the life that grows in a fracture, with each glyph germinating, blooming, withering and finally fissuring across its five variants. The foundry frames it as a system built to slow down reading rather than serve it.

name: Feroniapi
designer: Peter Wiegel, with the contribution of Julienne Richard
classification_notes: A redesign of Peter Wiegel's Feronia, drawn by Julienne Richard for the visual identity of Strasbourg's Palais des Fêtes. Art Nouveau curves and popular dance references shape the letters, softened for accessibility.
summary: An Art Nouveau-flavoured display italic redrawn from Peter Wiegel's Feronia, built for a Strasbourg dance venue.
description: Feroniapi began as Julienne Richard's redesign of Peter Wiegel's Feronia, commissioned for the identity of the Palais des Fêtes, an Art Nouveau dance hall in Strasbourg. Curved, sociable letterforms nod to the venue's architecture and to popular dance culture. The set carries frieze-pattern flourishes, fruit and vegetable dingbats and a set of post-binary ligatures.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne frames Feroniapi as a redesign of Peter Wiegel's Feronia, drawn while developing the Palais des Fêtes identity and inspired by Art Nouveau curves and popular dance. The foundry notes its post-binary ligatures, vowel variations and Art Nouveau frieze patterns.

name: Interlope
classification_notes: Modelled on the hand-drawn lettering from the cover of Interlopes, a magazine published by Lyon's Homosexual Liberation Group in the late 1970s. Keeps the DIY, amateur calligraphic character of the source rather than smoothing it into a polished script.
summary: A script typeface built from the amateur calligraphy on the cover of a 1970s French gay liberation magazine.
description: Interlope revives the hand-lettered cover of Interlopes, a magazine put out by Lyon's Homosexual Liberation Group between 1977 and 1979. Gabriel Dubourg kept the DIY spirit of the original amateur calligraphy rather than refining it away. A wide range of ligatures and ornamental alternates lets the digital font mimic the fantasy of the original.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Interlope as inspired by lettering from the first issue of Interlopes, a 1970s magazine of Lyon's Homosexual Liberation Group, drawn in an amateur calligraphic DIY style typical of the independent gay press of the period. The digital font keeps those qualities and adds a large range of ligatures and ornamental alternates.

name: Letters
classification_notes: Grew out of three years of research into how paper is depicted in print, tearing and burning paper by hand before tracing the results into Bézier curves. Torn and Lavish styles carry the material grain of paper into vector letterforms.
summary: A display face that renders the torn, burnt texture of paper in vector curves, the product of three years of material research.
description: Letters comes out of Céline Hurka and Jules Janssen's long-running interest in how paper is depicted in print, from teared ribbons to ornamental backgrounds. Three years of burning paper, digging through the Huis van het Boek archive and tracing photographs fed into an intentionally illogical design process. Torn and Lavish styles push that material grain into large-format vector display type.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Letters as derived from a historical interest in how paper is depicted in printed matter, aiming to render the material quality of paper through vectors. The typeface followed an organic, illogical process of burning paper, archive research and endless Bézier refinement.

name: Velvelyne
designer: Mariel Nils, Manon Van der Borght, with the contribution of Raphaël Bastide, Benjamin Dumond
classification_notes: Grew from a script-generated skeleton based on Liberation Sans into a four-weight stroke font. Built specifically as the house typeface for the Velvetyne website itself.
summary: A four-weight single-line stroke sans built by Velvetyne's own designers for their website.
description: Velvelyne started life as an algorithmically generated skeleton based on Liberation Sans, then grew a stroke and expanded into four weights, from Light to Bold. Mariel Nils and Manon Van der Borght built it as the house typeface for the Velvetyne site itself, with a set of post-binary ligatures folded in along the way.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Velvelyne as a typeface designed for its own website, evolving from a script-generated skeleton based on Liberation Sans into a stroke font across four weights, with a few post-binary ligatures added.

name: Sligoil
designer: Ariel Martín Pérez, with the contribution of Đông Trúc Nguyễn
classification_notes: Designed for the interface of the indie game Unknown Number, drawing on British Isles culture and the lettering of vintage MIT Space Cadet keyboards. Large inktraps and upright italic alternates keep it playful rather than utilitarian.
summary: A funky monospaced display face built for an indie video game, with large inktraps and a nod to vintage MIT keyboards.
description: Sligoil was drawn by Ariel Martín Pérez for the interface of the indie game Unknown Number, taking cues from British Isles culture and the lettering on vintage MIT Space Cadet keyboards. Large inktraps and upright italic alternates give it a distinctly playful monospaced character. A 2025 update added Vietnamese support with help from Đông Trúc Nguyễn.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Sligoil as a monospace typeface originally built for the interface of the indie videogame Unknown Number, drawing on the culture of the British isles and the letters of vintage MIT Space Cadet keyboards, with wide language support and a set of alternate forms.

name: Pilowlava
designer: Anton Moglia, Jérémy Landes, with the contribution of Maksym Kobuzan
classification_notes: Named for pillow lava, the smooth rounded rock formed when lava cools underwater. Compass-drawn geometry meets calligraphic, graffiti-informed hand dynamics, producing alternating letter shapes the foundry calls thermic accidents.
summary: A geometric display face that recalls cooled lava flows, balancing compass-drawn precision against calligraphic, graffiti-informed energy.
description: Pilowlava takes its name from pillow lava, the smooth rounded rock that forms when underwater volcanic flows cool. Anton Moglia and Jérémy Landes let calligraphic and graffiti hand movements disturb an otherwise geometric, compass-built structure, producing letters that alternate shape in what the foundry calls thermic accidents. A 3D variant and a climbing-gym edition with drilled holds have followed the original release.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Pilowlava as recalling cooled lava flows drawn with a compass, balancing viscous energy against controlled geometry, with hand-written and calligraphic dynamics producing alternating letter shapes and thermic accidents across the text.

name: Ouvrières
classification_notes: Designed during a variable-typography course at La Cambre in Brussels. Two variable axes let the letterforms shift between six named states, likened to a colony of worker ants adapting their formation.
summary: A variable display face where letterforms shift along two axes like a colony of ants adapting their formation.
description: Ouvrières treats its variable axes as a colony of worker ants, hungry, exploring, fighting or full, each state reshaping the letters into one of its named variants. Laure Azizi built it in 2023 during Eugénie Bidaut's variable typography course at La Cambre in Brussels, and the organic, assembled quality of the forms carries the insect metaphor through.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Les Ouvrières as a variable typeface where ants swarm through the forest for crumbs, sometimes hungry, sometimes fighters, adapting their formations along two variable axes into styles built to suit any situation.

name: Lineal
designer: Frank Adebiaye, with the contribution of Anton Moglia, Ariel Martín Pérez
classification_notes: Built from modules on a strict grid with no optical correction applied, giving it a Futura-like geometry stripped of the usual compensations. Anton Moglia later filled out the lowercase and weight range; a 2023 pass by Ariel Martín Pérez added language coverage.
summary: A modular geometric sans built without optical correction, closer to Futura reduced to its raw grid logic.
description: Lineal started as Frank Adebiaye's modular take on geometric sans construction, assembled from repeating units with no optical adjustment softening the result. Anton Moglia later added a full lowercase and extended the weight range from Thin to Heavy, and a 2023 revision by Ariel Martín Pérez broadened language support and tightened the spacing and kerning.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Lineal as a libre family initiated by Frank Adebiaye and updated by the Velvetyne team, drawn originally in FontForge on modular principles, since expanded with a fuller lowercase, more weights and wider language support.

name: BianZhiDai
classification_notes: Shading logic borrowed from ASCII art combines with the woven texture of Chinese plastic tote bags. Multiple COLR colour variants sit alongside plain outline versions.
summary: A modular display and colour font that borrows its shading logic from ASCII art and the woven texture of plastic tote bags.
description: BianZhiDai takes its texture from two sources: the shading conventions of ASCII art and the woven pattern of Chinese plastic tote bags. Xiaoyuan Gao built the letters from repeating modules, then released them across thirteen variants, from plain outline sets to full COLR colour fonts.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes BianZhiDai as an open-source font whose look draws on the shading characters of ASCII art and the texture of Chinese woven plastic bags, offered in colour and outline variants.

name: Jgs font
classification_notes: A tribute to Joan G. Stark, pioneer of ASCII art, drawn so its bitmap-like glyphs combine edge to edge into continuous lines, curves, frames and grey values. Released in sizes tuned to specific pixel multiples.
summary: A tribute to ASCII art pioneer Joan G. Stark, built as a monospaced bitmap face whose glyphs chain into continuous lines and patterns.
description: Jgs font honours Joan G. Stark, known as jgs or Spunk, an early pioneer of ASCII art. Adel Faure built it specifically for drawing ASCII art, with a bitmap look that blurs the line between text and image. Glyphs are designed to combine from one character to the next, producing continuous lines, curves, frames and grey values, and the family ships in sizes tuned to specific pixel multiples so the combinations stay aligned.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Jgs font as a tribute to Joan G. Stark, pioneer of ASCII art, specifically designed to draw ASCII art with a bitmap look whose shapes accentuate the ambiguity between text and drawing, combining across characters and lines into continuous patterns.

name: Fungal
classification_notes: Two variable axes, named grow and thickness, let the letterforms expand and contract like a spreading organism. Grew out of the fungal.page project, itself a homage to Wikipedia and early web collaboration.
summary: A variable sans whose grow and thickness axes let letters spread and swell like a fungal colony.
description: Fungal came out of Raphaël Bastide and Jérémy Landes' fungal.page project, a collaborative homage to Wikipedia and early web ideals. Two variable axes, grow and thickness, push the letterforms through instances that read like an organism expanding across a surface, and the character set stretches to Greek, Armenian, Georgian and Cyrillic alongside Latin.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Fungal as an open-source variable typeface made for the fungal.page project, paying homage to Wikipedia and early web ideals, with grow and thickness axes shaping its organic variation.

name: Lithops
classification_notes: Uppercase-only and hand-drawn in Procreate before being rebuilt in Glyphs, aiming for a font that is complex yet cohesive and legible. Named after lithops succulents, with loose nods to Art Nouveau, Matisse cutouts and irregular organic form.
summary: An uppercase-only fantasy display face, hand-drawn in Procreate and named after the succulent it echoes in form.
description: Lithops takes its name from the pebble-like succulent plant and its loose inspiration from Art Nouveau ornament and Matisse's cutouts. Anne-Dauphine Borione drew it first in Procreate before rebuilding it in Glyphs, working uppercase-only through a semi-modular structure that stays surprisingly cohesive despite its complexity. It sets out to test how complex a font can get while staying legible, and fun.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Lithops as a very display, very complex semi-modular font, uppercase only, hand-drawn in Procreate then processed in Glyphs, exploring how complex a font can be while staying cohesive, legible and fun.

name: Grotesk
designer: Frank Adebiaye, with the contribution of Ariel Martín Pérez
classification_notes: A heavily geometric sans with unusually wide spacing and a subtle art-deco flavour. The 2023 revision added a multiplexed weight system so paragraph width stays fixed as weight changes, plus a new lowercase and Russian, Ukrainian and Tifinagh support.
summary: A wide-spaced geometric grotesque with a subtle art-deco flavour, rebuilt in 2023 with multiplexed weights and broader script support.
description: Grotesk pairs heavy geometric construction with unusually generous spacing, giving it a relaxed, slightly art-deco character. Frank Adebiaye drew the original in 2010; Ariel Martín Pérez's 2023 revision added multiplexed weights, so switching weight leaves paragraph width untouched, alongside a new lowercase and support for Russian, Ukrainian and Tifinagh. An earlier version was used on the Paris city government's website.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Grotesk as a heavily geometric sans serif with unusually large spacing, its 2023 update introducing multiplexed weights that keep paragraph width fixed, subtle optical corrections, a new lowercase and support for Russian, Ukrainian, Tifinagh and further Latin-based languages.

name: Basteleur
classification_notes: Bold, ball-terminalled slab serif with a blobby cooperblack-like character, designed around the Tarot de Marseille's Magician card. A 2022 update added a lighter, sharper weight alongside the original bold.
summary: A bold, ball-terminalled slab serif drawn with the Tarot de Marseille's Magician card in mind.
description: Basteleur takes its name and its bulbous, cooperblack-flavoured character from Le Bateleur, the Magician of the Tarot de Marseille. Keussel built a blend of medieval-tinged and slab-serif forms around that card's lemniscate hat shape. A 2022 update added Moonlight, a lighter and sharper weight, alongside the original bold.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Basteleur as designed with the Tarot de Marseille in mind, producing a blend of medieval-ish and cooperblack-ish forms, with a 2022 update adding a lighter, sharper weight beside the original bold.

name: Degheest
designer: Ange Degheest, Camille Depalle, Eugénie Bidaut, Luna Delabre, Mandy Elbé, May Jolivet, Oriane Charvieux, Benjamin Gomez, Justine Herbel
subcategory: multi-family revival collection spanning serif, sans, mono and pixel
classification_notes: A revival project spanning several distinct sub-families, Abordage, Basalte, Director, Equateur, FT88 and Latitude among them, built after students found Ange Degheest's archive at the Rennes School of Fine Arts. Degheest (1928 to 2009) worked largely uncredited during her career, and the project exists to correct that.
summary: A revival collection reviving Breton lettering pioneer Ange Degheest's archive across several distinct display sub-families.
description: Degheest gathers together several sub-families, Abordage, Basalte, Director, Equateur, FT88 and Latitude among them, all drawn from letterer Ange Degheest's archive at the Rennes School of Fine Arts. Degheest worked through the second half of the twentieth century with little public recognition; a team of students rebuilt her drawings into working digital fonts as a way to finally credit her. The result spans serif, sans, pixel and near-monospace forms rather than sitting in one category.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes the Degheest project as born from discovering Ange Degheest's archives at the Rennes School of Fine Arts, mounting an exhibition and reviving her designs for free wide distribution as a way to finally honour her memory.

name: PicNic
classification_notes: Designed mainly for French, with contextual and inclusive ligatures that substitute midpoints automatically. Shapes take their cues from water drops on oilcloth and the shadows of leaves rather than from any serif tradition.
summary: An organic serif tuned for French, built around contextual and inclusive ligatures inspired by a picnic among friends.
description: PicNic reads sensory experience into type: the path of a water drop on oilcloth, tree-leaf shadows on a picnic blanket, an ant's route to a slice of watermelon. Mariel Nils built it mainly for French, with a cloud of contextual and inclusive ligatures that substitute the midpoint automatically. It came out as a co-release with NoFoundry, the student foundry of HfG Karlsruhe.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes PicNic as an organic typeface inhabiting a cloud of contextual and inclusive ligatures, mainly designed for French, its shapes drawn from the trajectory of a water drop on oilcloth and the shadows of leaves on a picnic blanket.

name: Amdal
classification_notes: Written in Tifinagh, the alphabet used for Tamazight (Berber), an ancient script that fell out of use before linguists and historians helped reintroduce it. Grew out of a lettering commission for a Sahara-inspired fashion collection.
summary: A Tifinagh titling face built to widen the small pool of digital type for the Tamazight alphabet.
description: Amdal means world in Tamazight, and Walid Bouchouchi built it in Tifinagh, the script used to write the Berber language across Algeria and Morocco. The project began as a lettering job for a Sahara-inspired fashion collection and grew into a fuller titling font covering Basic-IRCAM, Extended, Neo-Tifinagh and Touareg character sets. Few Tifinagh typefaces exist, and Amdal is meant as a starting point for others.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Amdal as a Tifinagh typeface whose alphabet fell into disrepair before being reintroduced through the work of regional linguists and historians, intended as an example and inspiration for typographers working in the script.

name: Façade
classification_notes: Traces its grid back to the facade of the ÉSAD Orléans building, originally drawn for the school's open-day identity. The Sud weight stays faithful to the architecture; the others drift further from it.
summary: A geometric display face traced from the architectural grid of the ÉSAD Orléans school facade.
description: Façade began as the visual identity for ÉSAD Orléans' open days, its first sketches lifted directly from the grid of the school building's facade. Éléonore Fines kept that grid as the spirit behind every weight: Sud stays close to the source architecture, while Ouest, Est and Sud Ouest pull further away. The name nods to façadisme, the practice of preserving only a building's exterior.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Façade as created from the architectural grid of the ÉSAD Orléans facade, used as the basis for its first sketches and then as a guiding spirit for every weight, with Sud staying faithful to the architecture while the others move away from it.

name: Gulax
designer: Morgan Gilbert, with the contribution of Anton Moglia
classification_notes: A single-weight monolinear sans the foundry itself introduces with a shrug, calling it just another experimental monolinear sans. No frills beyond a consistent single stroke weight throughout.
summary: A no-frills monolinear sans that the foundry shrugs off as just another experiment.
description: Gulax keeps a single, consistent stroke weight across every letter, with no serifs and no ornament to distract from the geometry. Morgan Gilbert first released it in 2014 and Anton Moglia contributed to a 2021 update, but the font's own tagline undersells it well enough: another experimental monolinear sans, take it or leave it.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne introduces Gulax simply as another experimental monolinear sans, inviting readers to enjoy it or not.

name: Outward
classification_notes: Originally capitals-only, drawn to erase white space and push toward solid black rather than the even grey typographers usually chase. Block, Round and Borders variants extend the same idea in different directions, with Cyrillic support alongside Latin.
summary: A capitals-first display sans built to maximise black ink coverage rather than chase an even typographic grey.
description: Outward Block set out to remove white space from capital letters altogether, pushing toward solid black type instead of the balanced grey typographers usually aim for. Raoul Audouin extended the idea into Round and Borders variants, each reworking the same dense geometry differently, with support reaching Cyrillic as well as Latin.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Outward Block as initially designed in capitals only, with the intent of getting rid of white space to reach a black type colour rather than the ideal grey typographers usually seek.

name: Anthony
classification_notes: Forms come from the way British sculptor Anthony Caro's metal pieces lean against each other. Pseudo-random alternates fire for most letters as you type, so no two lines read quite the same.
summary: A curveless display face inspired by sculptor Anthony Caro's leaning metal assemblages, with pseudo-random alternates on most letters.
description: Anthony reads sculpture into type, taking its angular, leaning forms from British sculptor Anthony Caro's metal assemblages. Sun Young Oh packed the family with alternates for most characters, pseudo-randomly substituted as you write, so the same word rarely repeats its shapes twice.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Anthony as inspired by artworks by British sculptor Anthony Caro, its forms coming from sculptures leaning against each other, packed with alternates for most letters that are pseudo-randomly picked as you write.

name: Mess
classification_notes: Framed by the designer as a critique of type foundries as opaque corporations. The specimen leans on politically charged text rather than a conventional character showcase.
summary: A brutalist display face framed as a quiet critique of the type foundry as an opaque corporation.
description: Mess sets out its own politics before its letterforms: the specimen frames a font as something like a corporation, hard to see into from outside. Tezzo Suzuki built the single Light weight around that idea, pairing raw brutalist shapes with politically charged specimen text rather than a neutral showcase.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne frames Mess through the designer's own words: font is something like a corporation, and from outside it is hard to see how it works and who is working in it.

name: Karrik
classification_notes: Deliberately keeps the weight disadjustments, missing optical corrections and uneven widths of early vernacular sans lettering. A stylistic set of chaotic uppercase alternates pays tribute to uneven garage lettering and obscure discontinued foundries.
summary: A vernacular grotesque that keeps the uneven widths and missing optical corrections of early sans lettering on purpose.
description: Karrik is rooted in vernacular typography, holding onto the weight disadjustments and uneven letter widths that mark early sans-serif lettering rather than correcting them away. Jean-Baptiste Morizot and Lucas Le Bihan added a stylistic set of chaotic, randomised uppercase forms as tribute to uneven garage signage and nameless, long-defunct foundries.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Karrik as rooted in vernacular typography, its weight disadjustments, lack of optical corrections and uneven letter widths a boundless reinterpretation of early sans serif features, with a stylistic set offering chaotic uppercase alternates as tribute to uneven garage lettering.

name: CirrusCumulus
classification_notes: Built entirely without curves from modules drawn from scientific diagrams. A lineal lowercase pairs with a script-like uppercase, and some glyphs switch to italic forms, throwing up unusual ligatures and arabesques.
summary: A curveless sans that pairs a lineal lowercase with a script-like uppercase, built from modules borrowed from scientific diagrams.
description: CirrusCumulus avoids curves entirely, building every letter from modules inspired by scientific diagrams. Clara Sambot hybridised two registers within one family: a lineal, geometric lowercase against a script-like uppercase, with some glyphs adopting italic forms that throw up unusual ligatures and arabesques. A large set of drawing characters and non-binary, inclusive glyphs rounds out the set.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes CirrusCumulus as designed without curves, made up of modules inspired by scientific diagrams, hybridising a lineal-style lowercase with a script-like uppercase, with a large panel of characters for drawing figures and shapes plus a variable ligature system and inclusive glyphs.

name: Mourier
designer: Eric Mourier, with the contribution of Sébastien Hayez, Ariel Martín Pérez, Alexander Kondratenko
classification_notes: Built on a strict 7x7 unit square and unclosed lines, first cast in lead for a 1971 booklet. Alexander Kondratenko later added Cyrillic capitals; Ariel Martín Pérez developed lowercase forms and diacritics for both scripts.
summary: A rigidly geometric alphabet built on a 7x7 unit grid of unclosed lines, revived from a 1971 lead-cast original.
description: Eric Mourier drew the original alphabet in 1971 to a strict set of rules: a 7 by 7 unit square grid and lines left deliberately unclosed. It first appeared cast in lead for the booklet The Myth about Bird B. Sébastien Hayez digitised it with Mourier's approval, Alexander Kondratenko later added Cyrillic capitals, and Ariel Martín Pérez filled out lowercase letters, diacritics and alternates for both scripts.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Mourier as a geometric alphabet designed by Eric Mourier in 1971 following a strict set of rules, based on a 7 by 7 unit square and made of unclosed lines.

name: Typefesse
classification_notes: Letters are drawn as folds of a body, readable only through the contortions of the figure they form. Claire-Obscure and Pleine variants trade off between graphic abstraction and plain legibility.
summary: A playful, body-shaped display face that reads through the folds and contortions of a figure rather than conventional letterforms.
description: Typefesse renders the alphabet through folds of the body, its contortionist letters hiding inside themselves or exposing themselves to the reader. Océane Juvin named the variants after lunar phases: Claire-Obscure keeps capitals in the more graphical Obscure style and lowercase in the more contorted Claire style, while Pleine strips the outlines back for maximum readability. It works as a titling face with a legibility that surprises at small sizes.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Typefesse as a playful, butt-shaped typeface where letters are rendered so that reading happens through the folds of the body, its contortionist creatures hiding inside or exposing themselves, creating confusion between reading, seeing and spying.

name: Kaeru Kaeru
classification_notes: Mixes the bright, blobby patterning of poison dart frogs with the exaggerated musculature of Japanese woodcuts. Made during a seminar at HfG Karlsruhe, co-released with the school's student foundry NoFoundry.
summary: An organic, blobby display face mixing poison dart frog patterning with the exaggerated musculature of Japanese woodcuts.
description: Kaeru Kaeru fuses two unlikely references: the bright, blob-patterned skin of poison dart frogs and the strangely muscular figures of Japanese woodcuts. Isabel Motz built it during a seminar at HfG Karlsruhe, released jointly with NoFoundry, the school's student-run foundry.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Kaeru Kaeru as bright coloured, blobby-shaped patterns of the poison dart frog mixed together with the strangely formed muscles in Japanese woodcuts.

name: Le Murmure
classification_notes: Commissioned as a custom titling face for French design agency Murmure, drawn with highly condensed proportions and a deliberate mismatch between characters for rhythm. Random OpenType substitution swaps in alternate letterforms. Won a Red Dot Grand Prix and a TDC Certificate of Excellence.
summary: A highly condensed titling sans commissioned for a French design agency, with random alternate letters keeping the rhythm unpredictable.
description: Le Murmure was drawn as a bespoke titling face for the French agency Murmure, condensed hard enough to sit comfortably in magazine-style headlines. Jérémy Landes of Studio Triple built in a deliberate rhythm of mismatched characters, and random OpenType substitution keeps swapping in more unusually drawn alternates. Alex Slobzheninov added Cyrillic and George Triantafyllakos added Greek. The design picked up a Red Dot Grand Prix and a TDC Certificate of Excellence.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Le Murmure as a typeface devoid of serifs combining effectiveness, legibility and singularity, created as a custom font for the agency Murmure, its highly condensed proportions playing on a skilful mismatch between characters to create a unique rhythm.

name: Ouroboros
designer: Ariel Martín Pérez, with the contribution of H·Alix Sanyas
classification_notes: Heavy, high-contrast serif forms carrying Art Nouveau ornament, built alongside a set of alchemical and astronomical symbols. Pitched at alchemists, witches and outsiders as much as typographers.
summary: A heavy, ornamental Art Nouveau display serif shipped with a set of alchemical and astronomical symbols.
description: Ouroboros leans into early Art Nouveau's own fondness for magical symbolism, pairing heavy, high-contrast serif letterforms with a full set of alchemical and astronomical glyphs. Ariel Martín Pérez pitches it at alchemists, witches, heretics and outsiders as readily as at typographers, with H·Alix Sanyas contributing to its development.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Ouroboros as a font for alchemists, witches, heretics, outsiders and curious people in general, inspired by early Art Nouveau styles once used alongside magical themes, coming together with a set of alchemical and astronomical symbols.

name: Format 1452
designer: Frank Adebiaye, with the contribution of Anton Moglia
classification_notes: A DIN-flavoured sans built from modules with no optical correction. The foundry's own line on the resulting quirks: it's not a bug, it's a feature.
summary: A DIN-flavoured modular sans built without optical correction, condensed and unapologetic about its quirks.
description: Format 1452 takes DIN's utilitarian character and rebuilds it from modules, skipping the optical correction that would normally smooth over the joins. Frank Adebiaye's condensed construction leaves the occasional rough edge in place deliberately, with the foundry shrugging off any resulting oddities as a feature rather than a bug.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Format 1452 as a Din-like typeface built with modules, without any optical corrections, noting plainly that it's not a bug, it's a feature.

name: BackOut
designer: Frank Adebiaye, with the contribution of Ariel Martín Pérez
classification_notes: Described by the foundry as a kind of African glyphic typeface, its name taken from Bob Marley's song of the same title.
summary: A bold African glyphic display face named after a Bob Marley song.
description: BackOut takes its name directly from Bob Marley's song, and Frank Adebiaye built the letters as a kind of African glyphic display face, bold and angular with an incised, carved quality rather than a drawn one.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes BackOut simply as a kind of African Glyphic typeface, its name referring to Bob Marley's eponymous song.

name: TINY
classification_notes: Modelled on the smallest type size of a HandJet EBS-250 textile printer, with a variable size axis controlling dot size across a wide range of instances. Six stylistic sets, small caps, fractions and roman numerals extend a punch-card-flavoured base.
summary: A variable dot-matrix monospace modelled on a textile printer's smallest type size, originally built for a Chinatown pop-up shop.
description: TINY began as the visual identity for an experimental pop-up shop in New York's Chinatown, its dot-based letterforms lifted from the smallest size setting of a HandJet EBS-250 textile printer. Jack Halten Fahnestock built a variable size axis that scales dot size across fifteen instances, backed by six stylistic sets, small caps, fractions and roman numerals across a set of more than 1,300 glyphs.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes TINY's variable dot size as coming from the HandJet's adjustable ink output, with designs that evoke punch card aesthetics across a large stylistic and glyph set.

name: Avara
designer: Raphaël Bastide, with the contribution of Wei Huang, Lucas Le Bihan, Walid Bouchouchi, Jérémy Landes
classification_notes: Nodes sit exclusively on a rough square grid, producing radical, constrained shapes for a transitional serif family. The grid-based method was chosen partly to make collaborative development easier.
summary: A curveless transitional serif built entirely on a rough square grid, its radical angularity a side effect of collaborative construction.
description: Avara restricts every node to a rough square grid, a constraint that pushes its transitional serif structure into radical, angular territory. Raphaël Bastide led the project with contributions from Wei Huang, Lucas Le Bihan, Walid Bouchouchi and Jérémy Landes, and the grid discipline was chosen partly to make the collaboration itself easier to manage across several hands.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Avara as a libre transitional serif curveless type family, its node placement based exclusively on a rough square grid, resulting in the radical and highly constrained shapes of the family.

name: VG5000
classification_notes: Named after the Philips home computer released in 1984, built on a grid four times finer than the machine's original 8x10 dot matrix. Deliberately keeps some angular vestiges of the source, including accents forced to a fixed height that make certain letters collide.
summary: A bold geometric sans that reworks the dot-matrix grid of the 1984 Philips VG5000 computer into contemporary curves.
description: VG5000 takes its name and its grid from the Philips home computer released in 1984, working on a matrix four times finer than the machine's original 8 by 10 dots to allow curves where the source only had right angles. Justin Bihan kept some of that heritage deliberately, including fixed-height accents that force certain letters to collide, the way they did on-screen. Working with artist Roxanne Maillet, the set also carries experimental glyphs for French inclusive writing.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes VG5000 as named after the homonymous 1984 Philips computer, built on a grid four times finer than its original dot matrix to allow more freedom of curve while retaining vestiges such as accents always placed at the same height, forcing some letters to crash.

name: Compagnon
designer: Juliette Duhé, Léa Pradine, Valentin Papon, Chloé Lozano, Sébastien Riollier
classification_notes: Five styles built from the online Typewriter Database archive, each weight referencing a different period in the history of typewriter type. Made at EESAB-Rennes as part of a graphic design masters programme.
summary: A five-style typewriter revival, each weight pulled from a different period of the Typewriter Database archive.
description: Compagnon draws its five styles from the online Typewriter Database, with each weight anchored to significant references from a different period in the history of typewriter faces. Juliette Duhé, Léa Pradine, Valentin Papon, Chloé Lozano and Sébastien Riollier built it together as part of EESAB-Rennes' graphic design masters programme, tracing the evolution of typewriter characters across the set.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Compagnon as a typeface family of five distinctive styles, finding its inspiration in the online archives of Typewriter Database specimens and combining different periods of the history of typewriter typefaces.

name: Trickster
classification_notes: Sharp, diamond-terminalled capitals give it a modern gothic character rather than a traditional textura blackletter. Built around the folkloric trickster archetype, a figure who uses secret knowledge to break normal rules.
summary: A modern gothic display face with sharp, diamond-terminalled letters, built around the folkloric trickster archetype.
description: Trickster takes its name and spirit from the trickster archetype, a folkloric figure, god or spirit who uses secret knowledge to disobey convention. Jean-Baptiste Morizot's letterforms carry a modern gothic edge, with sharp diamond terminals standing in for the traditional blackletter's calligraphic weight.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne frames Trickster around the folkloric archetype of a character exhibiting a great degree of intellect or secret knowledge, using it to play tricks or disobey normal rules and conventional behaviour.

name: Hyper Scrypt
classification_notes: Commissioned for the Hyper Chapelle exhibition, borrowing the stained-glass method of drawing light through holes in black lead. Letters are effectively drawn by their counters rather than their strokes, built on a rigorous grid for clean multi-line alignment.
summary: A reverse stencil display face borrowing the stained-glass method of drawing light through lead, commissioned for an exhibition near Metz cathedral.
description: Hyper Scrypt was commissioned by AAAAA Atelier for the Hyper Chapelle exhibition, and Jérémy Landes built it on the logic of stained glass: holes drawn for light, bordered in black lead, so the letters exist through their counters rather than their strokes. Despite that molten, organic look, a rigorous underlying grid keeps multi-line layouts cleanly aligned.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Hyper Scrypt as a modern stencil typeface inspired by the stained glass technique used in Metz cathedral, borrowing the stained glass method of drawing holes for light with black lead to create a reverse typeface whose letters are drawn by their counters.

name: Résistance
designer: A collective (Pauline Cormault, Esther Michaud, Claire Mucchieli, Merlin Andreae, Raphaël Maman, Pedro Gomes-Cardoso, Juliette Nier, Gabrielle Meistretty, Damien Bauza)
classification_notes: Also known on the foundry site as Résistance Générale. Built by ENSAD Paris students at La Générale using Glyphr Studio, exploring several meanings of résistance at once, historical, physical and electrical.
summary: A geometric curveless sans built collectively by ENSAD Paris students, its name playing on several meanings of resistance at once.
description: Résistance came out of a group of ENSAD Paris students working together at La Générale, building the family in Glyphr Studio. The name works on several registers at once: historical resistance, physical resistance and electrical resistance, and the geometric, curveless letterforms were a genuinely collective decision rather than one designer's hand.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne credits Résistance to a collective of ENSAD Paris students working at La Générale, exploring multiple interpretations of the word résistance, from historical to physical and electrical meanings.

name: Combat
classification_notes: Rebuilt from the ten letters of a single early twentieth-century newspaper masthead, Le Combat Social, an anarchist paper published in Limoges.
summary: An antique serif rebuilt from just ten letters of an early twentieth-century French anarchist newspaper masthead.
description: Combat exists because ten letters happened to survive: the masthead of Le Combat Social, an anarchist newspaper published in Limoges in the early twentieth century. A century later, Martin Desinde extended those ten letters into a full working serif, keeping the antique character of the original title lettering intact.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Combat as coming from an early twentieth-century anarchist newspaper published in Limoges called Le Combat Social, of which only the ten letters of the title were created for printing, the font now existing on its own a century later.

name: Steps Mono
classification_notes: Made for the French magazine Étapes as a demonstration of collaborative design, condensed and curveless in a utilitarian monospace mould.
summary: A condensed, curveless monospace built for the French magazine Étapes as a demonstration of two designers sharing one typeface.
description: Steps Mono was drawn for Étapes, the French design magazine, as a working demonstration of collaborative type design. Jean-Baptiste Morizot and Raphaël Bastide kept it condensed and curveless, favouring a utilitarian monospace mould over any display flourish.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne presents Steps Mono as a typeface made for the magazine Étapes to demonstrate a collaborative design process between its two designers.

name: Terminal Grotesque
designer: Raphaël Bastide, with the contribution of Jérémy Landes
classification_notes: Started as a side project while building a pixel font called Modulicon for a game, taking cues from Futura and Radim Peško's grotesque drawings. The designer treats it as a permanent beta, never meant to be finalised.
summary: A punk, pixel-inflected grotesque that its designer treats as a permanent beta, never meant to be finished.
description: Terminal Grotesque grew out of Raphaël Bastide's work on Modulicon, a pixel font for a game project, and settled into something closer to a cousin of pixel fonts: organic enough to read as text, punk and technical enough to keep its edge. Futura and Radim Peško's grotesque drawings both left a mark on the result. Bastide treats it deliberately as a beta project, open to perpetual modification rather than a finished release.
foundry_blurb: Velvetyne describes Terminal Grotesque as a cousin of pixel fonts enhanced enough to be organic while staying punk and technical, its beta status suited to perpetual modification rather than a finalised release.
